question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese commercial geography in India]
options: The Portuguese established their first factory (trading post) in India at – Calicut
The main spice exported from Malabar to Portugal was – black pepper
Goa became the headquarters of Portuguese commercial empire in Asia – after 1510
The Portuguese Estado da India was headquartered at – Calicut permanently after 1498
wrong_fact: The Portuguese Estado da India was NOT headquartered at Calicut. Goa (captured in 1510) became the permanent headquarters of Portuguese power in Asia. Calicut remained hostile and the Portuguese relied on Cochin initially before shifting to Goa.
explanation: The Portuguese Estado da India (State of India) established its permanent headquarters at Goa after Afonso de Albuquerque captured it in 1510. Calicut was never a stable Portuguese base – their factory there was destroyed in 1500. Cochin served as an early ally port. Goa's central location on the western coast and its excellent natural harbor made it ideal for controlling the Cape Route spice trade.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese commercial network in Asia]
options: Hormuz – controlled by Portuguese to dominate Persian Gulf trade
Malacca – captured by Portuguese in 1511 to control Southeast Asian spice trade
Diu – site of the decisive Portuguese naval victory in 1509 establishing Indian Ocean dominance
Aden – captured by Portugal to control Red Sea trade, completing the spice route blockade
wrong_fact: Portugal NEVER successfully captured Aden. Albuquerque attempted to take Aden in 1513 but failed. Aden remained under Yemeni/Ottoman control. The Portuguese failed to close the Red Sea route entirely, which is why the spice trade via the Red Sea/Egypt partially revived even after Portuguese dominance.
explanation: Portugal's 'golden triangle' strategy aimed at controlling Hormuz (Persian Gulf), Malacca (Southeast Asia), and Aden (Red Sea) to monopolize all Asian spice routes. They succeeded at Hormuz (1515) and Malacca (1511) and established dominance at Diu (1509 Battle), but FAILED to take Aden. This failure meant the Ottoman-controlled Red Sea route remained open, and Venice and Genoa continued to receive some spices via Egypt, limiting Portuguese monopoly.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese cartaz system and commercial geography]
options: Cartaz (permit) system – Portuguese naval licensing system for Indian Ocean trade ships
Portuguese charged cartaz fees at – key checkpoints like Goa, Hormuz, and Malacca
Ships without cartaz could be – seized or sunk by the Portuguese armada
The cartaz system was originally invented by – Arab merchants of the Red Sea as a protection racket
wrong_fact: The cartaz system was NOT invented by Arab merchants. It was a Portuguese innovation – a compulsory naval pass system they imposed on Indian Ocean trade. Ships had to purchase cartazes from Portuguese authorities or risk confiscation. It was a coercive instrument of Portuguese commercial hegemony, not an Arab institution.
explanation: The cartaz (from Portuguese 'carta' meaning letter/document) was a sea-pass system invented by the Portuguese to control Indian Ocean trade. All merchant ships – Arab, Indian, or other – had to purchase these passes from Portuguese officials at their fortified ports (Goa, Hormuz, Malacca, etc.). Ships found without a cartaz could be legally seized. This system was unique to the Portuguese and fundamentally different from earlier Arab trading practices, which were based on commercial agreements rather than naval coercion.
